bull_bear.body: All capital goes into stores and inventory; there was no dividend or buyback discussion. The structural feature investors must accept is that **95–98% of assets are inventory**, so operating cash flow is negative while the network grows. Management's defence: excluding working capital, cash profits from the P&L "are quite healthy," and OCF should turn positive as inventory productivity improves with scale. An analyst pushed back and stated plainly he did not agree — this is the sharpest unresolved disagreement on the call and belongs on the watch list. FOCO is partly a response: it adds network without adding D.P. capital.
bull_bear.title: Capital allocation

bull_bear.body:
- **The base effect is the central risk, and it was put to management directly.** Three quarters of gold-price-led growth will annualise into the base; if volume growth stays at 1–2%, reported growth collapses. Management's answer was behavioural, not numerical: sharp price rises cause customers to defer, stable prices bring deferred demand back. Gold ran to ~INR1,70,000–1,75,000, corrected to ~INR1,45,000–1,50,000, and demand is "gradually returning."
- **Import duty at 15%** (up from 6% in May 2026) — near-term cost and demand sensitivity, and the direct cause of the Q1 expansion pause.
- **Negative operating cash flow for three consecutive years**, disputed on the call.
- **New-store dilution.** New stores run at 3–4x asset turns versus 4.5–5x mature, so an accelerating roll-out mechanically drags blended productivity.
- **Diamond category declining** while being the stated margin lever — the March-2028 12–15% target requires a reversal, not a continuation.
- **National-brand competition in Tier-2/3** — management's rebuttal is the Indore density claim, which is unverifiable from outside.
- **Inventory carrying-value gap narrowing** — the ~20% cushion is a wasting asset.
bull_bear.title: Risks & watch-items

bull_bear.body: Substantive and, on the critical question, honest: the CFO volunteered unprompted that volume growth was only 1–2% and that just 10–15% of growth came from inventory gains — a disclosure that undercuts the headline and few managements would make. The store unit economics (breakeven months, turnover by format, inventory turns by store age) were given with unusual specificity, which makes them verifiable. Against that, the answers on the 51-store target were internally inconsistent within the same call — Manish Laddha said "five to seven will be FOCO," while Vikas Kataria said "around three to four franchise stores" and framed the 51 as all-COCO with franchising only *beyond* 51. The operating-cash-flow answer satisfied nobody. Tone on competition was confident to the point of bravado (the Indore comparison), and the team accepted a shareholder request to publish festive-season sales.
bull_bear.title: Management quality / tone

bull_bear.body:
- The business is structurally long the gold price through the making-charge mechanism, not just through inventory. Making charges are computed on the prevailing gold rate, so revenue and profitability rise with gold even at zero volume growth — which is precisely this quarter. Investors modelling this as a volume retailer will misread both the upside and the coming base effect.
- Old-gold exchange at 25% of sales is doing double duty: it improves customer affordability (funding purchases without fresh cash) *and* it is a natural hedge that reduces dependence on fresh gold procurement. Rising duty makes it structurally more valuable — a policy headwind that partially self-mitigates.
- Silver at +150% is the affordability release valve. Watch whether it keeps compounding if gold stays above INR1,50,000.
- The refusal to chase lower karatage is a deliberate positioning choice with a clear rationale (investment motive dominates in Tier-2/3), and it is the opposite of what several national peers are doing with 9-karat and 14-karat lines. It preserves realisation per gram but caps the affordability lever to lightweight designs only.
- The 51-store target has two mutually inconsistent descriptions on the same call. Treat 51 as the direction and the FOCO share as unresolved until the next quarter.
bull_bear.title: Non-obvious takeaways

bull_bear.body:
- Expansion has historically been through company-owned stores, with the growth pillar stating a "Strategic initiative to broaden its footprint throughout India via a self-owned outlets"; the Jabalpur store marks the first move to a FOCO (franchise-owned) model for asset-light expansion.
- Working-capital philosophy centres on cutting fresh gold purchases — old gold exchange contributed approximately 25% of total sales in Q1 FY27, and the Swarn Plus scheme forward-books demand.
- Financing and risk tools named are Gold Metal Loans (GMLs) and hedging at commodity exchange platforms, used to support margin stability and working capital efficiency.
- Real-estate light: of the 12 stores listed, only Indore (9,000 sq. ft.) is on owned premises; all others including the flagship Ratlam and Ratlam-II stores are on rented premises.

bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Gold price volatility and elevated gold prices weighing on demand volumes — Management describes a challenging operating environment with elevated gold prices and broader industry pressures influencing consumer sentiment and demand volumes, and states that these factors may influence purchase volumes in the short term. Mitigation is the proactive adoption of Gold Metal Loans (GML) and hedging mechanisms to manage price fluctuations, safeguard inventory and support margin stability. Read in the Chairman and Managing Director's message; the corresponding MD&A risk narrative reached this annual report set inside the capex_expansion bundle rather than the risks bundle.
- Inventory and working-capital intensity in a high gold-price environment — The MD&A notes that retailers face the challenge of maintaining adequate assortment and display stock while preserving liquidity, controlling borrowing costs, and avoiding product mix mismatches in a rapidly changing demand environment. This is a structural balance-sheet risk for a gold retailer. Text read in the MD&A industry section, which arrived in the capex_expansion bundle.
- Regulatory and import-duty risk on precious metals — The sector is described as highly sensitive to policy changes relating to imports, taxation, disclosure and compliance. After the close of FY26, India raised import tariffs on gold and silver to 15% in May 2026 from 6% earlier; such measures can raise landed cost, impact consumer affordability, and potentially encourage unofficial supply channels, while continued regulatory tightening increases operating complexity.
- Rural demand sensitivity and monsoon dependence — A significant portion of India's jewellery demand comes from rural and semi-urban markets where agricultural income, monsoon performance and crop realisations influence buying behaviour. As of May 2026 forecasts indicated a weaker monsoon outlook than the previous year, raising concerns for rural income growth and discretionary spending, particularly for weight-sensitive gold categories. This is structurally relevant given the Company's Tier II and Tier III, Central India footprint.
- Rapidly changing consumer preferences and mix shift away from weight-led gold — Demand is shifting toward lightweight jewellery, contemporary designs, daily wear, self-purchase categories and better perceived value, and part of discretionary spending is moving toward lab-grown diamonds, silver, digital gold and gold-linked investment products. This forces jewellers to refresh collections more frequently, reduce slow-moving inventory and balance traditional assortment against modern preferences.
- Competition from the unorganised sector and from other branded chains — The unorganised sector remains a strong competitive force through flexible pricing, local relationships and lower apparent making charges, while branded chains compete aggressively for wallet share via promotions, design differentiation, loyalty programmes and regional expansion. This creates a dual challenge of competing on value perception while defending margins.
- Skilled manpower availability and supply chain constraints — The industry depends on skilled karigars, designers and trained store personnel; availability of skilled artisans remains a challenge as design complexity rises. Fragmented supply chains and longer replenishment cycles can affect speed-to-market, assortment freshness and operational efficiency, especially for retailers scaling across multiple regions and store formats. The BRSR separately flags supply chain management as a risk of disruption and ethical sourcing challenges leading to delivery delays, lost sales and reputational damage.
- Customer privacy, data security and cyber risk — The BRSR material-issues table identifies customer confidentiality as a substantial peril, where unauthorised access or a security breach to critical information can cause financial losses, identity theft and loss of customer confidence, harming reputation, with legal penalties and fines as the stated negative financial implication. Mitigations cited are stringent data privacy policies, restricted access, password protection, firewalls, dedicated server rooms and periodic IT security review. The Directors' Report adds that cyber security maturity is reviewed periodically and that no incidents, breaches or loss of data occurred during the year.
- Access and affordability - balancing affordable options against perceived value and margin — The BRSR identifies this as a risk: companies must offer affordable options while upholding the perceived value of products and avoiding a race to the bottom, with a potential risk of impacting sales due to the challenge of balancing affordability and maintaining profit margins. Mitigations cited are new physical stores and economies of scale, strategic material procurement, and a customer-centric approach to pricing.
- Geographic and single-activity concentration — Structural concentration disclosed in BRSR Section A: markets served number 4 national states with zero international countries, exports are NIL as a percentage of turnover, the footprint is 12 showrooms and 4 offices with no plants, and gold and jewellery alone contribute 94.38% of total turnover. The business is therefore concentrated in one product category, one country and a small number of states.
bull_bear.title: Bear — key risks

business.body:
- **Gold (91% of revenue)** — 22-karat is ~80% of gold jewellery inventory, 18-karat ~15%, the balance 14-karat and below. Management is deliberately *not* pushing customers down the karat ladder; instead it engineers **lightweight 22-karat** designs, because Tier-2/3 customers treat jewellery as an investment first and a fashion accessory second, and prefer purity when a lightweight option exists.
- **Silver (+150%)** — the standout growth category, benefiting from gold-price-driven substitution.
- **Diamond/studded** — the only category to decline. At 6–7% of mix versus a 12–15% March-2028 target, this is the deliberate mix-upgrade lever. Management framed it as "a separate division which has to grow at its own path," to be over-weighted in specific cities (Bhilwara, Udaipur, Bhopal, Ujjain and larger upcoming cities) where higher inventory exposure should improve conversion and EBITDA. **Lab-grown diamonds: not being pursued** — judged unsuitable for Tier-2/3 because they carry no investment value and would not be accepted for bridal.
- **Amoura** — daily-wear lightweight studded sub-brand launched ~2 years ago, with dedicated counters in all showrooms.
- **Category mix by occasion:** wedding **62%**, festive/lightweight **18%**, other/gift articles **20%**.
- **Omni-channel** — e-commerce website and mobile app launched this quarter on both Play Store and App Store, plus expansion onto leading marketplaces. Management is careful not to over-claim: jewellery buying remains "largely relationship-driven and store-driven"; digital is for discovery and recall.
business.title: Segment / subsidiary detail

business.body:
- **Density economics that management quantified.** In Indore, a leading national jewellery brand runs ~14–15 stores across formats, and "the combined revenue of those stores is still lower than the revenue generated by a single D.P. store." That is the single most striking competitive claim on the call and, if accurate, explains why national-brand entry into Tier-2/3 is not automatically a threat.
- **86-year legacy and exchange credibility.** The buyback/exchange proposition is the practical moat in a market where jewellery is bought as investment: customers know they will get fair value at D.P. in five or ten years. Certified diamond jewellery realises within ~5–10% across jewellers, so the differentiation is the trust attached to the initial pricing.
- **Store-level productivity.** Mature stores turning inventory 8–9x versus a 4.7–5.0x company average.

latest_quarter.body:
EBITDA margin rose 80bps to 11.01% on scale, operating leverage, cost discipline and mix. The mechanism deserves attention: the business earns **making charges calculated on the prevailing gold price**, so a higher gold price mechanically raises absolute making-charge realisation even at flat volume — which is exactly what happened. Management added that over the last three to four months it optimised product mix toward SKUs that command better making charges. Normal gross margin was given as **10–11%** at the product level, with different margin profiles across gold, silver and diamond. The ~20% gap between carrying-value inventory (INR1,20,000 WAC) and market price is a real but *diminishing* tailwind as fresh procurement at INR1,45,000–1,50,000 dilutes the average.

Hedging is layered and was explained in preference order: (1) **real-time replenishment** — three to four bookings a day with vendors at the same price as the sale; (2) **old-gold exchange** as a natural hedge, now 25% of sales; (3) **Gold Metal Loan** backing 100% of any additional inventory; (4) **MCX positions** taken on analyst signals. The Board has approved comprehensive risk-management policies.

Swarna Plus** scheme launched in April 2026 — a gold SIP with a minimum INR5,000/month ticket running 10–11 months, where each monthly instalment buys gold weight at that day's price and is redeemable in bullion or jewellery at completion, giving the customer price protection. Because the scheme runs ~10 months from April, its sales contribution lands **post January–February 2027** — management confirmed this timing explicitly.

outlook.body:
- **Geographic adjacency expansion** — entering new states only where brand recall already exists, within a **100–200 km radius** of existing stores. Dahod is ~100 km from Ratlam and already has a D.P. customer base, which is what made it the Gujarat entry point. Maharashtra is being evaluated via Nagpur. **No metro plans.**
- **FOCO as an asset-light second gear** — Jabalpur is the pilot. Structure is revenue-sharing where D.P. retains full operational control ("entire control, operating procedures, management, SOPs will be of D.P.") and the franchisee takes a return plus the gold gain. Rationale: D.P.'s store formats are large and capital-heavy ("It is not INR5 crores, INR10 crores of showroom"), so franchising conserves capital in markets where D.P.'s own presence is not essential.
- **Studded mix upgrade** — the clearest margin lever available.
- **Swarna Plus** — locks in future purchase intent and smooths gold-price risk for the customer.
- **Brand-building** — Madhya Pradesh League Scindia Cup 2026 sponsorship; launch of the Rani Rupmati Collection (showcased in Kota).
outlook.title: Growth verticals / optionality

outlook.body:
- Expand with market intelligence: strengthen presence across Gujarat, Maharashtra, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan through a disciplined, research-led approach informed by regional market dynamics and customer preferences.
- Accelerate omnichannel growth: broaden customer reach through an integrated digital strategy, with the e-commerce website already launched, the mobile application in final testing and presence being expanded across leading online marketplaces.
- Scale through proven execution: build on the successful launch of stores in Ajmer, Neemuch, Ratlam and Dhar as a foundation for replicating the expansion model in new markets.
- Drive the COCO model: expand through a Company-Owned, Company-Operated model to maintain greater control over operations, inventory, pricing and customer experience, complemented by a Franchisee-Owned, Company-Operated (FOCO) format at Jabalpur for asset-light expansion.
- Enhance capital efficiency: reduce reliance on fresh gold procurement through gold exchange programmes and structured gold savings accumulation schemes, supporting working capital efficiency and enabling sustained sales even in a high gold-price environment.
- Strengthen product mix: increase focus on diamond-studded jewellery as a strategic growth category to enhance revenue contribution and strengthen the overall product portfolio.
- Manage gold price volatility: increase adoption of Gold Metal Loans (GML) and hedging mechanisms to manage commodity price fluctuations and support margin stability.
- Build a scalable, omnichannel jewellery retail platform through disciplined expansion, enhanced customer reach and prudent capital management, combining market-led store expansion with digital capabilities, inventory optimisation and a greater focus on high-value product categories.
- Strengthen customer engagement and demand through festivals, exhibitions and purchase-led initiatives, and through structured monthly accumulation schemes such as D. P. Swarn Plus and gold exchange programmes that enhance affordability.

outlook.body: Expansion is described as a key pillar of long-term growth, pursued through a disciplined, research-led approach to entering high-potential markets. During FY2025-26 the Company strengthened its retail presence across Central India with a new showroom at Dhar, following an earlier expansion in Ratlam, taking the total showroom network to 12; BRSR Section A reports 12 showrooms and 4 offices across 16 national locations and zero plants. Also during the year the Company finalised locations for three new showrooms, with all key agreements, approvals and formalities completed and fit-out activities underway, and all three are expected to become operational shortly: Jodhpur, Rajasthan under the Company-Owned, Company-Operated (COCO) model with a retail area of approximately 3,200-5,700 sq. ft. as shown for the three destinations, marking expansion into Rajasthan; Jabalpur, Madhya Pradesh, the first showroom there, under the Franchisee-Owned, Company-Operated (FOCO) model supporting an asset-light expansion strategy; and Dahod, Gujarat under the COCO model marking entry into Gujarat, with the Dahod showroom to be launched on September 24, 2026. The three destinations are stated with total retail areas of approximately 3,200 sq. ft., approximately 3,750 sq. ft. and approximately 5,700 sq. ft. respectively, though the report does not state which area belongs to which city. Beyond bricks and mortar the Company launched its official e-commerce platform during the year, with the mobile application in final testing and presence being expanded across leading online marketplaces, and states it intends to strengthen presence across Gujarat, Maharashtra, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan. Dividend was withheld for FY2025-26 expressly to preserve resources in view of planned business growth and various business expansion plans in the near future.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- Management sees the long-term structural growth potential of the Indian jewellery market supported by rising consumer aspirations, wedding-led demand, increasing preference for organised and trusted jewellers, and the gradual shift towards branded jewellery.
- Elevated gold prices, evolving consumer preferences and near-term demand considerations continue to shape the jewellery industry and may influence purchase volumes in the short term.
- Formalisation and growing preference for branded jewellery, supported by tighter regulatory compliance, hallmarking expansion and rising consumer awareness of purity and transparency; by May 2026 the number of districts under the hallmarking regime had increased to 385, favouring organised retailers over informal operators.
- A shift from weight-led purchases to design-led, lightweight, contemporary and utility-led jewellery, as high gold prices encouraged customers to stay within fixed spending budgets by opting for lighter pieces and exchange-based purchases; this creates opportunity in lightweight bridal, festive, office-wear, gifting and everyday-wear collections.
- Penetration into Tier II and Tier III markets remains one of the biggest structural opportunities; CRISIL noted that despite pressure on volumes in FY26, organised gold jewellery retailers are still expected to deliver healthy revenue growth supported by premium realisations, continued formalisation and deeper expansion in Tier II and Tier III cities.
- Omni-channel engagement and changing consumer discovery patterns, with purchase journeys increasingly influenced by digital discovery, social media visibility, online catalogues and store-assisted omni-channel experiences, while final conversion remains trust-led.
- Management states the long-term outlook for the Indian jewellery market remains favourable, supported by cultural relevance, rising aspirations, formalisation and increasing preference for trusted organised brands, but that growth is becoming more nuanced, with success increasingly dependent on design agility, inventory discipline, digital engagement, regional understanding and prudent capital management.
- Store-level demand drivers cited by management: strong customer footfalls, healthy conversion rates and enduring brand trust supported steady revenue growth.
- D. P. Swarn Plus, a structured 10-month gold accumulation programme starting at Rs 5,000 per month, strengthens demand visibility and customer engagement by creating a forward pipeline of committed jewellery purchases; redemption between 301 and 330 days carries up to 40% discount on gold making charges and up to 50% discount on diamond making charges.
- Three new showrooms (Jodhpur, Jabalpur, Dahod) have locations finalised with all key agreements, approvals and formalities completed and fit-out activities underway, and are expected to become operational shortly.
outlook.title: Demand & outlook drivers

deepdive.thesis: A headline that reads spectacular (+58% revenue, +77% PAT, 52% SSSG) but is almost entirely price, not volume — management disclosed volume growth of just **1–2%**, with the rest coming from higher gold prices flowing into making-charge realisation. The genuinely encouraging items sit underneath: EBITDA margin expanded 80bps to 11.01%, silver revenue grew 150%, old-gold exchange funded 25% of sales, and the store roll-out toward 51 outlets by FY30 restarted after a May pause following the **gold import duty hike from 6% to 15%**. The bear case is arithmetical — once the gold-price base catches up in two or three quarters, 10% volume growth is all that is left.

risks.note: Management describes a challenging operating environment with elevated gold prices and broader industry pressures influencing consumer sentiment and demand volumes, and states that these factors may influence purchase volumes in the short term. Mitigation is the proactive adoption of Gold Metal Loans (GML) and hedging mechanisms to manage price fluctuations, safeguard inventory and support margin stability. risks.risk: Gold price volatility and elevated gold prices weighing on demand volumes

risks.note: The MD&A notes that retailers face the challenge of maintaining adequate assortment and display stock while preserving liquidity, controlling borrowing costs, and avoiding product mix mismatches in a rapidly changing demand environment. This is a structural balance-sheet risk for a gold retailer. Text read in the MD&A industry section, which arrived in the capex_expansion bundle.
risks.risk: Inventory and working-capital intensity in a high gold-price environment

risks.note: The sector is described as highly sensitive to policy changes relating to imports, taxation, disclosure and compliance. After the close of FY26, India raised import tariffs on gold and silver to 15% in May 2026 from 6% earlier; such measures can raise landed cost, impact consumer affordability, and potentially encourage unofficial supply channels, while continued regulatory tightening increases operating complexity.
risks.risk: Regulatory and import-duty risk on precious metals

risks.note: A significant portion of India's jewellery demand comes from rural and semi-urban markets where agricultural income, monsoon performance and crop realisations influence buying behaviour. As of May 2026 forecasts indicated a weaker monsoon outlook than the previous year, raising concerns for rural income growth and discretionary spending, particularly for weight-sensitive gold categories. This is structurally relevant given the Company's Tier II and Tier III, Central India footprint.
risks.risk: Rural demand sensitivity and monsoon dependence

risks.note: Demand is shifting toward lightweight jewellery, contemporary designs, daily wear, self-purchase categories and better perceived value, and part of discretionary spending is moving toward lab-grown diamonds, silver, digital gold and gold-linked investment products. This forces jewellers to refresh collections more frequently, reduce slow-moving inventory and balance traditional assortment against modern preferences.
risks.risk: Rapidly changing consumer preferences and mix shift away from weight-led gold

risks.note: The unorganised sector remains a strong competitive force through flexible pricing, local relationships and lower apparent making charges, while branded chains compete aggressively for wallet share via promotions, design differentiation, loyalty programmes and regional expansion. This creates a dual challenge of competing on value perception while defending margins.
risks.risk: Competition from the unorganised sector and from other branded chains

risks.note: The industry depends on skilled karigars, designers and trained store personnel; availability of skilled artisans remains a challenge as design complexity rises. Fragmented supply chains and longer replenishment cycles can affect speed-to-market, assortment freshness and operational efficiency, especially for retailers scaling across multiple regions and store formats. The BRSR separately flags supply chain management as a risk of disruption and ethical sourcing challenges leading to delivery delays, lost sales and reputational damage.
risks.risk: Skilled manpower availability and supply chain constraints

risks.note: The BRSR material-issues table identifies customer confidentiality as a substantial peril, where unauthorised access or a security breach to critical information can cause financial losses, identity theft and loss of customer confidence, harming reputation, with legal penalties and fines as the stated negative financial implication. Mitigations cited are stringent data privacy policies, restricted access, password protection, firewalls, dedicated server rooms and periodic IT security review. The Directors' Report adds that cyber security maturity is reviewed periodically and that no incidents, breaches or loss of data occurred during the year.
risks.risk: Customer privacy, data security and cyber risk

risks.risk: Gold price volatility and elevated gold prices weighing on demand volumes
risks.note: Management describes a challenging operating environment with elevated gold prices and broader industry pressures influencing consumer sentiment and demand volumes, and states that these factors may influence purchase volumes in the short term. Mitigation is the proactive adoption of Gold Metal Loans (GML) and hedging mechanisms to manage price fluctuations, safeguard inventory and support margin stability. Read in the Chairman and Managing Director's message; the corresponding MD&A risk narrative reached this annual report set inside the capex_expansion bundle rather than the risks bundle.

risks.risk: Inventory and working-capital intensity in a high gold-price environment
risks.note: The MD&A notes that retailers face the challenge of maintaining adequate assortment and display stock while preserving liquidity, controlling borrowing costs, and avoiding product mix mismatches in a rapidly changing demand environment. This is a structural balance-sheet risk for a gold retailer. Text read in the MD&A industry section, which arrived in the capex_expansion bundle.

risks.risk: Regulatory and import-duty risk on precious metals
risks.note: The sector is described as highly sensitive to policy changes relating to imports, taxation, disclosure and compliance. After the close of FY26, India raised import tariffs on gold and silver to 15% in May 2026 from 6% earlier; such measures can raise landed cost, impact consumer affordability, and potentially encourage unofficial supply channels, while continued regulatory tightening increases operating complexity.

risks.risk: Rural demand sensitivity and monsoon dependence
risks.note: A significant portion of India's jewellery demand comes from rural and semi-urban markets where agricultural income, monsoon performance and crop realisations influence buying behaviour. As of May 2026 forecasts indicated a weaker monsoon outlook than the previous year, raising concerns for rural income growth and discretionary spending, particularly for weight-sensitive gold categories. This is structurally relevant given the Company's Tier II and Tier III, Central India footprint.

risks.risk: Rapidly changing consumer preferences and mix shift away from weight-led gold
risks.note: Demand is shifting toward lightweight jewellery, contemporary designs, daily wear, self-purchase categories and better perceived value, and part of discretionary spending is moving toward lab-grown diamonds, silver, digital gold and gold-linked investment products. This forces jewellers to refresh collections more frequently, reduce slow-moving inventory and balance traditional assortment against modern preferences.

risks.risk: Competition from the unorganised sector and from other branded chains
risks.note: The unorganised sector remains a strong competitive force through flexible pricing, local relationships and lower apparent making charges, while branded chains compete aggressively for wallet share via promotions, design differentiation, loyalty programmes and regional expansion. This creates a dual challenge of competing on value perception while defending margins.

risks.risk: Skilled manpower availability and supply chain constraints
risks.note: The industry depends on skilled karigars, designers and trained store personnel; availability of skilled artisans remains a challenge as design complexity rises. Fragmented supply chains and longer replenishment cycles can affect speed-to-market, assortment freshness and operational efficiency, especially for retailers scaling across multiple regions and store formats. The BRSR separately flags supply chain management as a risk of disruption and ethical sourcing challenges leading to delivery delays, lost sales and reputational damage.

risks.risk: Customer privacy, data security and cyber risk
risks.note: The BRSR material-issues table identifies customer confidentiality as a substantial peril, where unauthorised access or a security breach to critical information can cause financial losses, identity theft and loss of customer confidence, harming reputation, with legal penalties and fines as the stated negative financial implication. Mitigations cited are stringent data privacy policies, restricted access, password protection, firewalls, dedicated server rooms and periodic IT security review. The Directors' Report adds that cyber security maturity is reviewed periodically and that no incidents, breaches or loss of data occurred during the year.

risks.risk: Access and affordability - balancing affordable options against perceived value and margin
risks.note: The BRSR identifies this as a risk: companies must offer affordable options while upholding the perceived value of products and avoiding a race to the bottom, with a potential risk of impacting sales due to the challenge of balancing affordability and maintaining profit margins. Mitigations cited are new physical stores and economies of scale, strategic material procurement, and a customer-centric approach to pricing.

Structural concentration disclosed in BRSR Section A: markets served number 4 national states with zero international countries, exports are NIL as a percentage of turnover, the footprint is 12 showrooms and 4 offices with no plants, and gold and jewellery alone contribute 94.38% of total turnover. The business is therefore concentrated in one product category, one country and a small number of states.

one-line thesis: A headline that reads spectacular (+58% revenue, +77% PAT, 52% SSSG) but is almost entirely price, not volume — management disclosed volume growth of just **1–2%**, with the rest coming from higher gold prices flowing into making-charge realisation. The genuinely encouraging items sit underneath: EBITDA margin expanded 80bps to 11.01%, silver revenue grew 150%, old-gold exchange funded 25% of sales, and the store roll-out toward 51 outlets by FY30 restarted after a May pause following the **gold import duty hike from 6% to 15%**. The bear case is arithmetical — once the gold-price base catches up in two or three quarters, 10% volume growth is all that is left.

> Adjustments / one-offs: (a) **Only ~10–15% of the growth came from inventory gains** — the majority is higher making charges on a higher gold price. (b) Inventory carries at a weighted-average cost of ~INR1,20,000 versus a prevailing pure-gold price of ~INR1,51,000–1,52,000 — a **~20% embedded gap** that will narrow as fresh purchases at INR1,45,000–1,50,000 enter the base. (c) **Gold import duty was raised from 6% to 15% in May 2026**, which is why Q1 store expansion was deliberately paused. (d) Operating cash flow has been negative for three years — management attributes this to inventory being 95–98% of assets; an analyst on the call explicitly declined to accept the explanation.
guidance (critical — verify next quarter:
- **Volume growth: ~10% for both FY27 and FY28** — the single most important number on the call, and the metric management says it manages to internally ("what matters most is how many kilograms or tonnes of jewellery we have sold"). Value growth is explicitly left to the gold price.
- **Margin:** no explicit target. Mix-led improvement expected from a higher studded share and better making-charge products.
- **Store roll-out:** **51 stores by FY30** (from 12 today) — "we will continue with our vision of 51 stores, there is no doubt." **~5–6 new stores in FY27**; **6–8 stores per year from FY28 through FY30**. Mix: majority COCO, with **~5–7 FOCO** across the 51 and **2–3 franchisees per year**, the FOCO pilot running for four to five years.
- **Studded mix:** from **6–7% today to 12–15% by March 2028** — i.e. "at least 2x to 3x of what we have today of diamond segment."
- **Near-term store pipeline:** Dahod (Gujarat, ~3,200 sq ft, COCO — Gujarat entry) and Jabalpur (MP, ~3,750 sq ft, first FOCO) have all agreements and approvals complete, fit-outs underway, "operational soon." Two more locations under active planning, and management expected to **finalise another two to three locations by end-July 2026**.
- **Store unit economics (a checkable promise):** capex breakeven in **6–9 months**; an 8,000–10,000 sq ft store to reach **INR350–400 cr turnover** in 3–4 years; a smaller 3,000–5,000 sq ft store **INR150–200 cr**. Inventory turns progress ~3x after 2–3 years, 4.5–5x after 4–5 years, 8–9x for stores past 6–7 years.
- **Disclosure commitment:** management agreed to start publishing **festive-season sales updates** from the August festival season onward.
order book & pipeline: Not applicable. The forward-revenue proxies are the store pipeline (above) and the **D.P. Swarna Plus** scheme launched in April 2026 — a gold SIP with a minimum INR5,000/month ticket running 10–11 months, where each monthly instalment buys gold weight at that day's price and is redeemable in bullion or jewellery at completion, giving the customer price protection. Roughly **50 customers are contributing above INR1,00,000 per month**, spread across all showrooms rather than concentrated geographically. Because the scheme runs ~10 months from April, its sales contribution lands **post January–February 2027** — management confirmed this timing explicitly.
segment / subsidiary detail:
- **Gold (91% of revenue)** — 22-karat is ~80% of gold jewellery inventory, 18-karat ~15%, the balance 14-karat and below. Management is deliberately *not* pushing customers down the karat ladder; instead it engineers **lightweight 22-karat** designs, because Tier-2/3 customers treat jewellery as an investment first and a fashion accessory second, and prefer purity when a lightweight option exists.
- **Silver (+150%)** — the standout growth category, benefiting from gold-price-driven substitution.
- **Diamond/studded** — the only category to decline. At 6–7% of mix versus a 12–15% March-2028 target, this is the deliberate mix-upgrade lever. Management framed it as "a separate division which has to grow at its own path," to be over-weighted in specific cities (Bhilwara, Udaipur, Bhopal, Ujjain and larger upcoming cities) where higher inventory exposure should improve conversion and EBITDA. **Lab-grown diamonds: not being pursued** — judged unsuitable for Tier-2/3 because they carry no investment value and would not be accepted for bridal.
- **Amoura** — daily-wear lightweight studded sub-brand launched ~2 years ago, with dedicated counters in all showrooms.
- **Category mix by occasion:** wedding **62%**, festive/lightweight **18%**, other/gift articles **20%**.
- **Omni-channel** — e-commerce website and mobile app launched this quarter on both Play Store and App Store, plus expansion onto leading marketplaces. Management is careful not to over-claim: jewellery buying remains "largely relationship-driven and store-driven"; digital is for discovery and recall.
growth verticals / optionality:
- **Geographic adjacency expansion** — entering new states only where brand recall already exists, within a **100–200 km radius** of existing stores. Dahod is ~100 km from Ratlam and already has a D.P. customer base, which is what made it the Gujarat entry point. Maharashtra is being evaluated via Nagpur. **No metro plans.**
- **FOCO as an asset-light second gear** — Jabalpur is the pilot. Structure is revenue-sharing where D.P. retains full operational control ("entire control, operating procedures, management, SOPs will be of D.P.") and the franchisee takes a return plus the gold gain. Rationale: D.P.'s store formats are large and capital-heavy ("It is not INR5 crores, INR10 crores of showroom"), so franchising conserves capital in markets where D.P.'s own presence is not essential.
- **Studded mix upgrade** — the clearest margin lever available.
- **Swarna Plus** — locks in future purchase intent and smooths gold-price risk for the customer.
- **Brand-building** — Madhya Pradesh League Scindia Cup 2026 sponsorship; launch of the Rani Rupmati Collection (showcased in Kota).
6a. moat & competitive position:
- **Density economics that management quantified.** In Indore, a leading national jewellery brand runs ~14–15 stores across formats, and "the combined revenue of those stores is still lower than the revenue generated by a single D.P. store." That is the single most striking competitive claim on the call and, if accurate, explains why national-brand entry into Tier-2/3 is not automatically a threat.
- **86-year legacy and exchange credibility.** The buyback/exchange proposition is the practical moat in a market where jewellery is bought as investment: customers know they will get fair value at D.P. in five or ten years. Certified diamond jewellery realises within ~5–10% across jewellers, so the differentiation is the trust attached to the initial pricing.
- **Store-level productivity.** Mature stores turning inventory 8–9x versus a 4.7–5.0x company average.
margins & cost dynamics:
EBITDA margin rose 80bps to 11.01% on scale, operating leverage, cost discipline and mix. The mechanism deserves attention: the business earns **making charges calculated on the prevailing gold price**, so a higher gold price mechanically raises absolute making-charge realisation even at flat volume — which is exactly what happened. Management added that over the last three to four months it optimised product mix toward SKUs that command better making charges. Normal gross margin was given as **10–11%** at the product level, with different margin profiles across gold, silver and diamond. The ~20% gap between carrying-value inventory (INR1,20,000 WAC) and market price is a real but *diminishing* tailwind as fresh procurement at INR1,45,000–1,50,000 dilutes the average.

Hedging is layered and was explained in preference order: (1) **real-time replenishment** — three to four bookings a day with vendors at the same price as the sale; (2) **old-gold exchange** as a natural hedge, now 25% of sales; (3) **Gold Metal Loan** backing 100% of any additional inventory; (4) **MCX positions** taken on analyst signals. The Board has approved comprehensive risk-management policies.

FY27 target ~5–6 stores; FY28–FY30 at 6–8 per year to reach 51. Management conceded the pace has been uneven — "in a year one it may be instead of eight it will be six, but in the year two and year three it will be compensated" — because the May 2026 duty hike forced a deliberate Q1 slowdown.
capital allocation: All capital goes into stores and inventory; there was no dividend or buyback discussion. The structural feature investors must accept is that **95–98% of assets are inventory**, so operating cash flow is negative while the network grows. Management's defence: excluding working capital, cash profits from the P&L "are quite healthy," and OCF should turn positive as inventory productivity improves with scale. An analyst pushed back and stated plainly he did not agree — this is the sharpest unresolved disagreement on the call and belongs on the watch list. FOCO is partly a response: it adds network without adding D.P. capital.
risks & watch-items:
- **The base effect is the central risk, and it was put to management directly.** Three quarters of gold-price-led growth will annualise into the base; if volume growth stays at 1–2%, reported growth collapses. Management's answer was behavioural, not numerical: sharp price rises cause customers to defer, stable prices bring deferred demand back. Gold ran to ~INR1,70,000–1,75,000, corrected to ~INR1,45,000–1,50,000, and demand is "gradually returning."
- **Import duty at 15%** (up from 6% in May 2026) — near-term cost and demand sensitivity, and the direct cause of the Q1 expansion pause.
- **Negative operating cash flow for three consecutive years**, disputed on the call.
- **New-store dilution.** New stores run at 3–4x asset turns versus 4.5–5x mature, so an accelerating roll-out mechanically drags blended productivity.
- **Diamond category declining** while being the stated margin lever — the March-2028 12–15% target requires a reversal, not a continuation.
- **National-brand competition in Tier-2/3** — management's rebuttal is the Indore density claim, which is unverifiable from outside.
- **Inventory carrying-value gap narrowing** — the ~20% cushion is a wasting asset.
management quality / tone: Substantive and, on the critical question, honest: the CFO volunteered unprompted that volume growth was only 1–2% and that just 10–15% of growth came from inventory gains — a disclosure that undercuts the headline and few managements would make. The store unit economics (breakeven months, turnover by format, inventory turns by store age) were given with unusual specificity, which makes them verifiable. Against that, the answers on the 51-store target were internally inconsistent within the same call — Manish Laddha said "five to seven will be FOCO," while Vikas Kataria said "around three to four franchise stores" and framed the 51 as all-COCO with franchising only *beyond* 51. The operating-cash-flow answer satisfied nobody. Tone on competition was confident to the point of bravado (the Indore comparison), and the team accepted a shareholder request to publish festive-season sales.
non-obvious takeaways:
- The business is structurally long the gold price through the making-charge mechanism, not just through inventory. Making charges are computed on the prevailing gold rate, so revenue and profitability rise with gold even at zero volume growth — which is precisely this quarter. Investors modelling this as a volume retailer will misread both the upside and the coming base effect.
- Old-gold exchange at 25% of sales is doing double duty: it improves customer affordability (funding purchases without fresh cash) *and* it is a natural hedge that reduces dependence on fresh gold procurement. Rising duty makes it structurally more valuable — a policy headwind that partially self-mitigates.
- Silver at +150% is the affordability release valve. Watch whether it keeps compounding if gold stays above INR1,50,000.
- The refusal to chase lower karatage is a deliberate positioning choice with a clear rationale (investment motive dominates in Tier-2/3), and it is the opposite of what several national peers are doing with 9-karat and 14-karat lines. It preserves realisation per gram but caps the affordability lever to lightweight designs only.
- The 51-store target has two mutually inconsistent descriptions on the same call. Treat 51 as the direction and the FOCO share as unresolved until the next quarter.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: D. P. Abhushan Limited is engaged in the business of manufacturing, sale and trading of Gold Jewellery, Diamond Jewellery, Platinum Jewellery, Silver Jewellery and other precious Metals. It operates a Business-to-Consumer (B2C) retail model, sourcing jewellery from reputable suppliers and jewellers and selling directly to end consumers through its own network of retail showrooms, while also undertaking jewellery manufacturing and design services on a need or customisation basis. Under a smaller B2B model it caters to corporate clients by issuing gift cards or coins and serves businesses engaged in the same industry.

demand_drivers.body:
- Management sees the long-term structural growth potential of the Indian jewellery market supported by rising consumer aspirations, wedding-led demand, increasing preference for organised and trusted jewellers, and the gradual shift towards branded jewellery.
- Elevated gold prices, evolving consumer preferences and near-term demand considerations continue to shape the jewellery industry and may influence purchase volumes in the short term.
- Formalisation and growing preference for branded jewellery, supported by tighter regulatory compliance, hallmarking expansion and rising consumer awareness of purity and transparency; by May 2026 the number of districts under the hallmarking regime had increased to 385, favouring organised retailers over informal operators.
- A shift from weight-led purchases to design-led, lightweight, contemporary and utility-led jewellery, as high gold prices encouraged customers to stay within fixed spending budgets by opting for lighter pieces and exchange-based purchases; this creates opportunity in lightweight bridal, festive, office-wear, gifting and everyday-wear collections.
- Penetration into Tier II and Tier III markets remains one of the biggest structural opportunities; CRISIL noted that despite pressure on volumes in FY26, organised gold jewellery retailers are still expected to deliver healthy revenue growth supported by premium realisations, continued formalisation and deeper expansion in Tier II and Tier III cities.
- Omni-channel engagement and changing consumer discovery patterns, with purchase journeys increasingly influenced by digital discovery, social media visibility, online catalogues and store-assisted omni-channel experiences, while final conversion remains trust-led.
- Management states the long-term outlook for the Indian jewellery market remains favourable, supported by cultural relevance, rising aspirations, formalisation and increasing preference for trusted organised brands, but that growth is becoming more nuanced, with success increasingly dependent on design agility, inventory discipline, digital engagement, regional understanding and prudent capital management.
- Store-level demand drivers cited by management: strong customer footfalls, healthy conversion rates and enduring brand trust supported steady revenue growth.

margins.title: Margins & cost dynamics
margins.body:
EBITDA margin rose 80bps to 11.01% on scale, operating leverage, cost discipline and mix. The mechanism deserves attention: the business earns **making charges calculated on the prevailing gold price**, so a higher gold price mechanically raises absolute making-charge realisation even at flat volume — which is exactly what happened. Management added that over the last three to four months it optimised product mix toward SKUs that command better making charges. Normal gross margin was given as **10–11%** at the product level, with different margin profiles across gold, silver and diamond. The ~20% gap between carrying-value inventory (INR1,20,000 WAC) and market price is a real but *diminishing* tailwind as fresh procurement at INR1,45,000–1,50,000 dilutes the average.

Hedging is layered and was explained in preference order: (1) **real-time replenishment** — three to four bookings a day with vendors at the same price as the sale; (2) **old-gold exchange** as a natural hedge, now 25% of sales; (3) **Gold Metal Loan** backing 100% of any additional inventory; (4) **MCX positions** taken on analyst signals. The Board has approved comprehensive risk-management policies.

capital_allocation.title: Capital allocation
capital_allocation.body: All capital goes into stores and inventory; there was no dividend or buyback discussion. The structural feature investors must accept is that **95–98% of assets are inventory**, so operating cash flow is negative while the network grows. Management's defence: excluding working capital, cash profits from the P&L "are quite healthy," and OCF should turn positive as inventory productivity improves with scale. An analyst pushed back and stated plainly he did not agree — this is the sharpest unresolved disagreement on the call and belongs on the watch list. FOCO is partly a response: it adds network without adding D.P. capital.

capex_expansion.body: Expansion is described as a key pillar of long-term growth, pursued through a disciplined, research-led approach to entering high-potential markets. During FY2025-26 the Company strengthened its retail presence across Central India with a new showroom at Dhar, following an earlier expansion in Ratlam, taking the total showroom network to 12; BRSR Section A reports 12 showrooms and 4 offices across 16 national locations and zero plants. Also during the year the Company finalised locations for three new showrooms, with all key agreements, approvals and formalities completed and fit-out activities underway, and all three are expected to become operational shortly: Jodhpur, Rajasthan under the Company-Owned, Company-Operated (COCO) model with a retail area of approximately 3,200-5,700 sq. ft. as shown for the three destinations, marking expansion into Rajasthan; Jabalpur, Madhya Pradesh, the first showroom there, under the Franchisee-Owned, Company-Operated (FOCO) model supporting an asset-light expansion strategy; and Dahod, Gujarat under the COCO model marking entry into Gujarat, with the Dahod showroom to be launched on September 24, 2026. The three destinations are stated with total retail areas of approximately 3,200 sq. ft., approximately 3,750 sq. ft. and approximately 5,700 sq. ft. respectively, though the report does not state which area belongs to which city. management_tone.title: Management quality / tone
management_tone.body: Substantive and, on the critical question, honest: the CFO volunteered unprompted that volume growth was only 1–2% and that just 10–15% of growth came from inventory gains — a disclosure that undercuts the headline and few managements would make. The store unit economics (breakeven months, turnover by format, inventory turns by store age) were given with unusual specificity, which makes them verifiable. Against that, the answers on the 51-store target were internally inconsistent within the same call — Manish Laddha said "five to seven will be FOCO," while Vikas Kataria said "around three to four franchise stores" and framed the 51 as all-COCO with franchising only *beyond* 51. The operating-cash-flow answer satisfied nobody. Tone on competition was confident to the point of bravado (the Indore comparison), and the team accepted a shareholder request to publish festive-season sales.

risks.title: Risks & watch-items
risks.body:
- **The base effect is the central risk, and it was put to management directly.** Three quarters of gold-price-led growth will annualise into the base; if volume growth stays at 1–2%, reported growth collapses. Management's answer was behavioural, not numerical: sharp price rises cause customers to defer, stable prices bring deferred demand back. Gold ran to ~INR1,70,000–1,75,000, corrected to ~INR1,45,000–1,50,000, and demand is "gradually returning."
- **Import duty at 15%** (up from 6% in May 2026) — near-term cost and demand sensitivity, and the direct cause of the Q1 expansion pause.
- **Negative operating cash flow for three consecutive years**, disputed on the call.
- **New-store dilution.** New stores run at 3–4x asset turns versus 4.5–5x mature, so an accelerating roll-out mechanically drags blended productivity.
- **Diamond category declining** while being the stated margin lever — the March-2028 12–15% target requires a reversal, not a continuation.
- **National-brand competition in Tier-2/3** — management's rebuttal is the Indore density claim, which is unverifiable from outside.
- **Inventory carrying-value gap narrowing** — the ~20% cushion is a wasting asset.

non_obvious.title: Non-obvious takeaways
non_obvious.body:
- The business is structurally long the gold price through the making-charge mechanism, not just through inventory. Making charges are computed on the prevailing gold rate, so revenue and profitability rise with gold even at zero volume growth — which is precisely this quarter. Investors modelling this as a volume retailer will misread both the upside and the coming base effect.
- Old-gold exchange at 25% of sales is doing double duty: it improves customer affordability (funding purchases without fresh cash) *and* it is a natural hedge that reduces dependence on fresh gold procurement. Rising duty makes it structurally more valuable — a policy headwind that partially self-mitigates.
- Silver at +150% is the affordability release valve. Watch whether it keeps compounding if gold stays above INR1,50,000.
- The refusal to chase lower karatage is a deliberate positioning choice with a clear rationale (investment motive dominates in Tier-2/3), and it is the opposite of what several national peers are doing with 9-karat and 14-karat lines. It preserves realisation per gram but caps the affordability lever to lightweight designs only.
- The 51-store target has two mutually inconsistent descriptions on the same call. Treat 51 as the direction and the FOCO share as unresolved until the next quarter.

Certified diamond jewellery realises within ~5–10% across jewellers, so the differentiation is the trust attached to the initial pricing.
- **Store-level productivity.** Mature stores turning inventory 8–9x versus a 4.7–5.0x company average.
margins & cost dynamics:
EBITDA margin rose 80bps to 11.01% on scale, operating leverage, cost discipline and mix. The mechanism deserves attention: the business earns **making charges calculated on the prevailing gold price**, so a higher gold price mechanically raises absolute making-charge realisation even at flat volume — which is exactly what happened. Management added that over the last three to four months it optimised product mix toward SKUs that command better making charges. Normal gross margin was given as **10–11%** at the product level, with different margin profiles across gold, silver and diamond. The ~20% gap between carrying-value inventory (INR1,20,000 WAC) and market price is a real but *diminishing* tailwind as fresh procurement at INR1,45,000–1,50,000 dilutes the average.

Hedging is layered and was explained in preference order: (1) **real-time replenishment** — three to four bookings a day with vendors at the same price as the sale; (2) **old-gold exchange** as a natural hedge, now 25% of sales; (3) **Gold Metal Loan** backing 100% of any additional inventory; (4) **MCX positions** taken on analyst signals. The Board has approved comprehensive risk-management policies.

| Dahod, Gujarat | ~3,200 sq ft | COCO | Agreements/approvals complete, fit-out underway — "operational soon"; marks Gujarat entry |

| 2 further locations | — | — | Under planning/discussion |
| 2–3 more | — | — | Targeted to be finalised by end-July 2026 |

FY27 target ~5–6 stores; FY28–FY30 at 6–8 per year to reach 51. Management conceded the pace has been uneven — "in a year one it may be instead of eight it will be six, but in the year two and year three it will be compensated" — because the May 2026 duty hike forced a deliberate Q1 slowdown.
capital allocation: All capital goes into stores and inventory; there was no dividend or buyback discussion. The structural feature investors must accept is that **95–98% of assets are inventory**, so operating cash flow is negative while the network grows. Management's defence: excluding working capital, cash profits from the P&L "are quite healthy," and OCF should turn positive as inventory productivity improves with scale. An analyst pushed back and stated plainly he did not agree — this is the sharpest unresolved disagreement on the call and belongs on the watch list. FOCO is partly a response: it adds network without adding D.P. capital.
risks & watch-items:
- **The base effect is the central risk, and it was put to management directly.** Three quarters of gold-price-led growth will annualise into the base; if volume growth stays at 1–2%, reported growth collapses. Management's answer was behavioural, not numerical: sharp price rises cause customers to defer, stable prices bring deferred demand back. Gold ran to ~INR1,70,000–1,75,000, corrected to ~INR1,45,000–1,50,000, and demand is "gradually returning."
- **Import duty at 15%** (up from 6% in May 2026) — near-term cost and demand sensitivity, and the direct cause of the Q1 expansion pause.
- **Negative operating cash flow for three consecutive years**, disputed on the call.
- **New-store dilution.** New stores run at 3–4x asset turns versus 4.5–5x mature, so an accelerating roll-out mechanically drags blended productivity.
- **Diamond category declining** while being the stated margin lever — the March-2028 12–15% target requires a reversal, not a continuation.
- **National-brand competition in Tier-2/3** — management's rebuttal is the Indore density claim, which is unverifiable from outside.
- **Inventory carrying-value gap narrowing** — the ~20% cushion is a wasting asset.
management quality / tone: Substantive and, on the critical question, honest: the CFO volunteered unprompted that volume growth was only 1–2% and that just 10–15% of growth came from inventory gains — a disclosure that undercuts the headline and few managements would make. The store unit economics (breakeven months, turnover by format, inventory turns by store age) were given with unusual specificity, which makes them verifiable. Against that, the answers on the 51-store target were internally inconsistent within the same call — Manish Laddha said "five to seven will be FOCO," while Vikas Kataria said "around three to four franchise stores" and framed the 51 as all-COCO with franchising only *beyond* 51. The operating-cash-flow answer satisfied nobody. Tone on competition was confident to the point of bravado (the Indore comparison), and the team accepted a shareholder request to publish festive-season sales.
non-obvious takeaways:
- The business is structurally long the gold price through the making-charge mechanism, not just through inventory. Making charges are computed on the prevailing gold rate, so revenue and profitability rise with gold even at zero volume growth — which is precisely this quarter. Investors modelling this as a volume retailer will misread both the upside and the coming base effect.
- Old-gold exchange at 25% of sales is doing double duty: it improves customer affordability (funding purchases without fresh cash) *and* it is a natural hedge that reduces dependence on fresh gold procurement. Rising duty makes it structurally more valuable — a policy headwind that partially self-mitigates.
- Silver at +150% is the affordability release valve. Watch whether it keeps compounding if gold stays above INR1,50,000.
- The refusal to chase lower karatage is a deliberate positioning choice with a clear rationale (investment motive dominates in Tier-2/3), and it is the opposite of what several national peers are doing with 9-karat and 14-karat lines. It preserves realisation per gram but caps the affordability lever to lightweight designs only.
- The 51-store target has two mutually inconsistent descriptions on the same call. Treat 51 as the direction and the FOCO share as unresolved until the next quarter.
